client: I've been feeling really anxious ever since my professor assigned this big group project. I keep worrying about having to present in front of the class, and the thought of messing up in front of everyone makes my stomach hurt. I'm not sure how talking about it will help when the real problem is that I just can't do public speaking.
therapist: It sounds like this project has been weighing heavily on you, especially the part about presenting in front of the class. You seem to feel stuck, unsure how to move past this worry. Let’s explore what’s behind the fear of public speaking—what thoughts come up when you imagine presenting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I imagine presenting, I just keep thinking, "What if I freeze up and forget everything?" or "What if everyone thinks I sound stupid?" It feels like my mind goes blank whenever I try to prepare, and I end up avoiding working on it altogether. I don’t know how to stop these thoughts—they just take over.
therapist: It seems like your mind is caught in a cycle of "what ifs," which can feel overwhelming and make it hard to focus on preparing. Let’s work on breaking those thoughts down—what’s the worst that could happen, and how might you cope if it did? Sometimes facing those fears head-on can help us feel more in control.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess the worst that could happen is I completely mess up and embarrass myself in front of everyone. I’m not sure how I’d cope with that—it feels like something I’d never recover from. Even thinking about it makes me want to avoid the project even more, but I know I can’t just skip it.
therapist: It sounds like the fear of embarrassment is really weighing on you, and it’s understandable to want to avoid something that feels so uncomfortable. Let’s explore this idea of “never recovering”—what would it mean to you if that happened? Sometimes our minds amplify the consequences, and unpacking that can help us see things more realistically.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if I embarrassed myself, it would mean everyone would think less of me, and I’d feel like I’ve failed. I know logically that it wouldn’t *actually* ruin my life forever, but in the moment, it feels so real and terrifying. It’s hard to shake that fear, even if I try to tell myself it’s not as bad as I’m imagining.
therapist: It’s good that you can recognize the difference between what your emotions are telling you and the logical reality—that’s an important first step. It sounds like the fear of judgment feels so intense in the moment, even if you know it’s unlikely to define your entire life. Let’s work on grounding those fears—what’s one small, manageable step you could take to feel more prepared and confident?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess one small step could be practicing my presentation in front of a friend or family member first, but honestly, even that feels daunting. I’m worried they’ll judge me too, even if they’re supportive. It’s hard to shake the feeling that I’ll mess up no matter what I do.
therapist: It sounds like even practicing in front of someone you trust feels overwhelming right now, which makes sense if you’re anticipating judgment. What if we started even smaller—maybe just practicing by yourself or recording your voice? That way, you can build confidence gradually without feeling the pressure of an audience.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Practicing by myself or recording my voice might be easier, but I still feel like it’s not the same as having real people there. I’m worried I’ll just freeze up when it’s time for the actual presentation, no matter how much I practice alone. It’s like my anxiety takes over, and I can’t control it.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to prepare and feeling like the anxiety will still take over when it really counts. That’s a frustrating place to be. What if we focus on building small moments of confidence first, rather than trying to control everything at once? Sometimes, breaking the fear into smaller pieces makes it feel less overwhelming.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess small moments of confidence might help, but I'm still not sure how that translates to actually standing in front of the class. What if all those little moments don't add up when it matters most? I feel like my anxiety is this huge wall I can't climb, no matter how small the steps are.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling stuck, worried that even small steps won’t be enough to overcome the anxiety when it’s time to present. That sense of the “wall” being too big to climb can feel really overwhelming. Let’s focus on what’s within your control—like how you respond to that anxiety—instead of trying to conquer it all at once. What’s one thing that might help you feel a little more grounded in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe taking deep breaths could help, but I've tried that before and it doesn't seem to do much when the panic really hits. I feel like my body just takes over and all the techniques go out the window. It's frustrating because I know these things are supposed to help, but they don't feel powerful enough against this kind of fear.
therapist: It sounds like you’ve tried using breathing techniques, but they haven’t felt effective when the panic really sets in. That frustration is completely valid—it can feel like your body is working against you in those moments. Let’s explore what happens when the panic hits—what does your body feel like, and what thoughts tend to come up? Sometimes understanding that pattern can help us find new ways to work with it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When the panic hits, my chest gets tight and my hands shake so much I can't hold my notes. The thoughts spiral into "I can't do this, I'm going to fail" on repeat. Even though I know it's irrational, in that moment it feels completely true and inescapable.
therapist: It sounds like in those moments of panic, your body and mind feel completely overwhelmed, and it’s hard to see a way out. Even though you know the thoughts are irrational, they feel so real and convincing when they take over. Let’s focus on grounding yourself in those moments—what’s one thing you can do to remind yourself that this feeling, while intense, is temporary?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, slow speech

client: Maybe I could try reminding myself that the panic will pass, but it’s hard to believe that in the moment. It feels like it’s never going to end, even though logically I know it will. I’m not sure if just telling myself that will be enough to calm me down when it’s happening.
therapist: It sounds like part of you knows the panic will pass, but in the moment, that reassurance feels hollow—almost like your mind doesn’t fully believe it. That disconnect can make the fear feel even more overwhelming. What if we paired that reminder with something physical, like pressing your feet firmly into the ground? Sometimes combining thoughts with actions can make coping strategies feel more tangible.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
